we have used exome sequencing to identify gene-level association signals for rare variants in four genes at exome-wide levels of significance and in 12 gene sets, including those for drug targets and candidate genes from mouse knockout experiments.

we identified gene-level associations of exome-wide significance for rare variants in 4 genes, including a series more than 30 SLC30A8 alleles and 12 gene sets, including those for T2D drug target and candidate genes from mouse knockout studies.

exome-sequenced data from 20,791 patients with type 1 diabetes and 24 440 controls from 5 ancestries identified gene level signals for rare variants that explain at most 1/4th of the heritabilities of the strongest common signals, and the strongest gene level signals in established type 1 diabetes drug targets will require more than 75,000-185,000 sequenced cases to achieve significance.

the results from this study provide evidence that rare variants in specific genes may be associated with type 1 diabetes, but that further research is needed to confirm these findings.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rare-variant gene-level association signals are modest in their effect sizes, but they can be harnessed to provide new insights into disease biology.
rare variants in established T2 diabetes drug targets are unlikely to provide the next major breakthrough for T2D therapeutics.

rare variants in established drug targets and genes from knockout mouse models are enriched for type 2 diabetes associations, but that these associations do not explain a large amount of the heritablity of the strongest single-variant associations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rare variants are unlikely to explain most of the genetic risk of type 2diabetes.

, while rare coding variants in protein-coding genes can be associated with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, the gene-level effect size of these rare coding variants is small and will require large numbers of sequenced cases to achieve statistical significance.
rare coding variants are unlikely to be responsible for a large fraction of the heritablity of type 2 diabeties, at least in the genes that we examined.
